title: Sarah Breeden: This time is different?
summary: Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden delivered a speech assessing financial system resilience and current vulnerabilities, concluding that while the banking system is considerably stronger than pre-GFC, risks have shifted to market-based finance and sovereign balance sheets. She highlighted three salient vulnerabilities: private markets, non-bank financial intermediaries, and sovereign debt exposure.
key_points: Global financial system has proved resilient through six major shocks in six years: pandemic, Ukraine war, overseas bank failures including a G-SIB, UK gilt market stress in 2022, trade disruptions, and energy shock
UK banks hold significantly more and higher-quality capital and liquidity than pre-GFC; resolution regimes reduce systemic risk from individual bank failures
Activity has migrated from banks to market-based finance, now accounting for roughly half of UK and global financial-sector assets
Global private-market assets under management have risen approximately six-fold since 2008/9, to roughly $18 trillion by 2025
Private markets have not been tested at this scale and complexity by a broad-based macroeconomic shock in a higher-rate environment
Public debt in advanced economies is now close to post-war highs, reducing fiscal space and increasing sensitivity to shifts in market confidence
Sovereign bond markets anchor pricing for mortgages and corporate credit, and provide core collateral for repo and derivatives markets
why_it_matters: This speech provides an authoritative BoE assessment of current financial stability vulnerabilities. It signals regulatory attention to private markets, non-bank leverage, and sovereign debt exposure as key risks. Market participants should note that the Deputy Governor explicitly connects sovereign bond market stress to broader financial system plumbing risks, referencing the UK 2022 gilt crisis as a cautionary example.
market_structure_context: The speech extensively discusses market structure vulnerabilities: (1) the shift from bank-based to market-based finance, now ~50% of financial assets; (2) private market opacity, leverage 'layer cake' at borrower/fund/sponsor levels, and limited transparency; (3) sovereign bond markets as core plumbing for repo and derivatives; (4) complex interconnections between private markets, banks, insurers, and reinsurers creating an ecosystem where losses become hard to trace; (5) recent default events (MFS, Tricolor, First Brands Group) reinforcing liquidity and asset quality concerns.

six-fold increase in private-market AUM since 2008/9
~50% of UK and global financial-sector assets now in market-based finance
post-war highs in advanced economy public debt
